cards.explanation: The answer is back home in Jerusalem. The text says it plainly: "…but David remained in Jerusalem." Joab, David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), is out there with the whole army, and the king is at home. The whole crew is on the job site, and the one in charge is still at the house. Keep that detail in your pocket, friends.

The answer is that she's the wife of Uriah the Hittite. David is told, "This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite." So David hears she's a married woman, and he hears her husband's name too. Hold on to that name, friends. Uriah is about to matter a lot.
The answer is pregnant. Bathsheba sends word to David: "I am pregnant." Just three words. This is where the story turns heavy, and everything David does next comes after he gets that message.

The answer is house. David says to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah has just come from the war, so it sounds like a king sending a tired man home. And a gift from the king follows him out. Keep your eyes on where Uriah actually ends up, friends.

The answer is at the palace door with the servants. The text says, "But Uriah slept at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants; he did not go down to his house." The king handed him a free night at home, and he chose the doorway. Somebody told David, too. David asks him about it next.

The answer is that Uriah can't go home to his house and his wife. He says, "How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?" The ark, Israel and Judah are in tents, and Joab's soldiers are out in the open field. So Uriah won't go to his own house, and he makes that clear to the king.

The answer is True. David says, "Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day and the next. That comes right after Uriah's answer about not going home.

The answer is False. Even after David got him drunk, the text says Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master's servants, and he did not go home. Once again he sleeps among the servants. The man stays put, friends.

The answer is to put him at the front of the fiercest battle. The letter says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." This part is heavy, friends. And Uriah carried that letter himself.

The answer is False. The letter says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." The order is to withdraw from him, not to stay close beside him.
The answer is that he dies in the battle. The text says, "…some of David’s servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite also died." It's a sad verse, friends. He wasn't the only one who fell that day.

The answer is why they got so close to the wall. Joab says the king may ask, "Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from atop the wall?" Joab tells the messenger what to say if that happens. He's thinking ahead, and he has an answer ready.

The answer is Uriah. Joab's instructions are for if the king asks why they got so close to the wall. Then the messenger is to say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well." That line comes after the question about Abimelech and the millstone.

The answer is that David tells Joab not to let this matter upset him. David says, "Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another." Joab had been ready for anger. What David sends is that line, followed by orders to strengthen the attack.

The answer is True. The text says, "When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him." It's a short verse about a real loss, friends. I think this one is just meant to be sat with.

The answer is evil. The passage closes with, "But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD." After all the letters, messages and orders, this is how the LORD sees what David did. The text says it straight, friends.
